name: Zoe Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Zoe. I'm a researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. To start, what's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a line crew for the electric co-op along the coast, so it's salt air, rusted hardware and a lot of storm damage. We replace corroded crossarms, fix lines after the winter gales, and work around a lot of trees, which is the one bit I actually know well. I'm second year, still learning, and I'm clumsy on the live-line tools, Birgit, our foreman, has to slow down for me more than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up here at 43?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Erik and I ran a landscaping and tree-trimming business for fifteen years, mostly gardens and hedges, and sometimes trees too close to power lines, which is how I met the co-op crews. Two years ago we sold it to a bigger firm, Erik stayed on part-time there, and I wanted a steady wage and a pension, so I applied. I still think like a business owner, I use AI every day, it did all our quotes and invoices, and now it helps me study and keeps my notes on every job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and nothing more, like a good chainsaw. At work I'd shrug, most of the crew never cared anyway. Online I'd maybe say I told you so to a few of the excitable ones at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get what I came for, a steady wage and a pension, and I learn the trade properly. The coast will always need its lines fixed after storms. I'd keep using the tools for the boring stuff, because they still save me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going with the apprenticeship, keep using AI for my study and notes. We've got about four months saved from the business sale after paying down the mortgage, and I'd keep adding to that. Maybe I'd do the odd weekend tree job with Erik for extra money, like old times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sold the business for a steady wage. Was that hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harder than I expected. I miss being my own boss, choosing the jobs, talking to customers. But the kids needed one parent with a regular payslip, and that's me now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Storm season, honestly, the long call-outs mean Freya ends up minding Nils. And whether I'm good enough to pass my next assessment. Ordinary things.

S0.say: It's a useful tool and nothing more, like a good chainsaw. I'd shrug at work and maybe tell a few excitable friends at church that I told them so.
S0.think: It means I get what I came for, a steady wage and pension, and I learn the trade properly. I'd keep using the tools for the boring stuff, because they still save me hours.
S0.do: Keeps going with her apprenticeship and daily AI use for study and job notes. Keeps adding to about four months of savings and does the occasional weekend tree job with her husband for extra money.
S0.quote: It's a useful tool and nothing more, like a good chainsaw.
S0.fieldNote: She still thinks like a business owner even as a junior employee. She traded independence for a payslip for her family's sake and misses being her own boss. AI is ordinary for her, a time-saver she has used for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is normal, every generation gets new tools and the ones who pick them up do well. I'd tell the crew not to moan, just learn it. I wouldn't want the government stepping in much, let businesses work it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I see an opportunity. The co-op spends a fortune on tree trimming near lines, and with drones and AI mapping you could plan that work much better. I know trees and I'm learning lines, that's a rare mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Birgit in the first month about joining any vegetation planning project the co-op starts. On weekends I'd start offering tree-risk surveys with a drone and AI mapping to farms and small businesses, Erik could do the cutting. I'd spend maybe a thousand on a decent drone and software, out of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, like when we landed our first big contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're junior on the crew. Could the change hurt you before it helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could, I'm not daft. If they need fewer climbers, I'm not the first name they'd keep. That's why I'd want a second string, my own little business, so I'm not putting all the eggs in the co-op basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Freya, who's 15?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a skill, and learn how to sell it. That's what my father told me, he had a bakery. It's still true, robots or not.

S1.say: This is normal: every generation gets new tools, and the ones who pick them up do well. Let businesses work it out without much government interference.
S1.think: I see an opportunity, because the co-op spends a fortune on tree trimming near lines and drones and AI mapping could plan it much better. I know trees and I'm learning lines, which is a rare mix.
S1.do: Asks her foreman in the first month to join any vegetation planning project. Spends about a thousand from savings on a drone and mapping software and starts weekend tree-risk surveys, with her husband doing the cutting.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like landing a first big contract.
S1.quote: I know trees and I'm learning lines, that's a rare mix.
S1.fieldNote: Her business instinct turns this picture into an opening around tree management near lines. She knows her junior status leaves her exposed and answers that with a side business rather than a complaint. Her free-market view shows in wanting government to stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock and families and communities need to stick together. I wouldn't be calling for the government to stop it, it can't be stopped. I'd be telling people at church to look after each other and think about what they can do, not just what they've lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job on the crew would be gone fast, I'm under no illusions. But if robots can do everything, someone still owns them and hires them out. I'd want to be on that side, even in a small way, though two years is very little time and I'm not sure I'd manage it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold onto cash first, no new car, no trips, get the savings up. Then I'd look into buying or leasing one of the first tree-cutting robots with Erik, and offer it to farms and the co-op, the same way we used to hire out our stump grinder. It's a risk, and I'd only do it if the numbers worked, but sitting still is a bigger risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a knot in my stomach. But also a bit of the old business adrenaline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the savings as big as possible and talk to the bank about what a small equipment loan would look like. Watch who's making the machines and what they cost. Two years is short, so I'd spend it getting ready to jump the day they're for sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a robot sounds like a big risk with a mortgage. How does Erik feel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, Zoe, we just sold one business, are you mad? And he'd have a point. We'd pray about it and do the sums together, and if the sums didn't work, I wouldn't do it.

S2.say: It's a huge shock, and families and communities need to stick together. It can't be stopped, so people should think about what they can do, not just what they've lost.
S2.think: My job on the crew would go fast, but someone still owns the robots and hires them out, and I'd want to be on that side. Two years is very little time, though, and I'm not sure I'd manage it.
S2.do: Holds cash, cuts the new car and trips, and builds savings while asking the bank about a small equipment loan. Looks into buying or leasing an early tree-cutting robot with her husband to hire out to farms and the co-op, but only if the numbers work.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her stomach, but also some of the old business adrenaline.
S2.quote: If robots can do everything, someone still owns them and hires them out.
S2.fieldNote: Even facing a fast job loss, she reaches for ownership rather than protection, modelled on hiring out the old stump grinder. She was honest that two years might be too short and that her husband would push back. Faith and family sums would decide the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so families and small businesses should start now. I'd want the government to keep regulations light so small outfits can buy the machines, not just big corporations. That's what I'd say at church and anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years suits me pretty well. I'd finish my ticket, grow the weekend survey work, and by 2031 I could have a small company that owns a couple of machines. If the co-op crew shrinks, I'd step out to the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship in two years. Build the tree survey business on weekends, put the profits aside, and around year three buy our first robot or a share in one with another family business. I'd keep my AI tools running the books, quotes and scheduling, like I did before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big job where you've done the planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have a business and a family. Who looks after the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Freya would be 20 by then, Nils 17, so less of that. My mother lives two streets away, and she'd love an excuse to see them more. Family's how we've always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Birgit, our foreman, she's brilliant but she's never used anything more than a flip phone. If the machines come, she'd need someone to show her. I'd offer, and she'd probably tell me to mind my own business.

S3.say: There's time to get ready, so families and small businesses should start now. The government should keep regulations light so small outfits can buy the machines, not just big corporations.
S3.think: Five years suits me pretty well: I'd finish my ticket, grow the survey work and could own a couple of machines by 2031. If the co-op crew shrinks, I'd step out to the business.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship in two years while building the weekend tree survey business and saving its profits. Around year three buys a first robot, or a share in one with another family business, and runs the books and scheduling with AI tools.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but in a good way, like before a well-planned big job.
S3.quote: I'd want the government to keep regulations light so small outfits can buy the machines, not just big corporations.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she plans a clear path from apprentice to small machine-owning business. Her political ask is light regulation that lets small family firms compete with big ones. She leans on her mother for childcare, in keeping with her family-first view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone with a bit of gumption can do something with it. Families should sit down and plan. I'd be fairly cheerful about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's the best of the three. I'd get eight years of steady wages and pension from the co-op while I build the business slowly on the side. By the time it lands, I'd be ready to step out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Qualify, then keep the co-op job and grow the weekend business slowly over five or six years. Buy the first machines once they're proven and the price drops, maybe year six or seven. Then step away from the co-op and run the business full-time, with Erik, and maybe Nils if he wants in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a plan I can actually see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with 2 or 5 years, what does the decade really change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be gambling. With five I'd be hurrying. With ten I'd be building, and building is what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about it that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether my kids will have something to do that makes them proud. I don't want them sitting at home while machines work. That's why I'd want them in the family business, doing something real.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and anyone with a bit of gumption can do something with it. Families should sit down and plan.
S4.think: For me it's the best of the three: eight years of steady wages and pension while I build the business slowly on the side. By the time it lands, I'd be ready to step out.
S4.do: Qualifies and keeps the co-op job while growing the weekend business over five or six years. Buys the first machines once they're proven and cheaper, around year six or seven, then leaves the co-op to run the business full-time with her husband and perhaps her son.
S4.feel: Calm, with a plan she can actually see.
S4.quote: With two years I'd be gambling. With five I'd be hurrying. With ten I'd be building, and building is what I'm good at.
S4.fieldNote: The decade turns her from anxious gambler to calm builder, and she is the one most ready to leave employment for ownership. Her remaining worry is about her children's sense of purpose, which she answers with a family business. Her plans consistently pair caution on money with appetite for new machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything, you'd just be grabbing. What would help is small businesses being able to get loans and buy the machines early, not just big companies, and the co-op being straight with its crews about what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who ends up owning the robots. Everyone asks who loses their job. I'd rather ask who gets to own the machine that took it, and whether a family like mine can be one of them.

headlineQuote: I'd rather ask who gets to own the machine that took it, and whether a family like mine can be one of them.
portrait: Zoe Hansen is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice on a coastal electricity co-op's line crew, after fifteen years running a landscaping and tree-trimming business with her husband Erik, which they sold two years ago. She has two teenagers, a mortgage and about four months of savings, and uses AI every day as she did for her business. She is traditional and free-market, trusts family, church and small business over government, and still thinks like an owner. She is calm through a plateau and steady change, anxious at AGI in two years, and calm again with a decade, when she plans to buy tree-cutting robots and run a family business. Her central question is who gets to own the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build anything, only to grab what she could.
whatWouldHelp: Small businesses being able to get loans and buy machines early rather than only big companies, and the co-op being straight with its crews about what's coming.
